newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechens say war will resume if Lebed removed.
newsitem.headline: Chechens say war will resume if Lebed removed.

text.p: Chechen separatist leaders said on Thursday that war would resume in their breakaway region if Russian President Boris Yeltsin sacked his controversial security chief Alexander Lebed.
Lebed, architect of a fragile Chechen peace deal, is embroiled in a vicious feud with Russian Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov and has been criticised by other top officials.
"If they get rid of Lebed, we will have to prepare for war because you can expect anything from people like Kulikov," separatist chief-of-staff Aslan Maskhadov told Reuters.

Kulikov has publicly blasted the deal, which postpones for five years a decision on the region's political status, saying it means caving in to separatist demands and marks a humiliating defeat for the Russian army.
On Wednesday Kulikov accused Lebed of planning to seize power in Moscow with the help of 1,500 Chechen fighters. Lebed denies the charges.
Maskhadov told Radio Russia that Kulikov's claim was untrue.
"We have no intention of getting involved in sorting out sordid squabbles in Moscow. We have enough on our plate," said Maskhadov, a co-signatory of Lebed's August 31 peace accord.
"We think that General Lebed is a realistic person who was the first to see that Russia and the people of Russia are in danger," he said.
"Kulikov, on the contrary, is a disgrace for the army and Russia," Maskhadov said.

Yeltsin, who is preparing for a heart operation, has not yet decided how to react to Kulikov's accusations but is concerned about some of Lebed's actions, presidential spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said on Thursday.
Rebel spokesman Movladi Udugov said he was confident that Lebed would survive the latest round of Kremlin mudslinging.
"His opponents will fail because, according to our information, Lebed is very popular with the Russian people," Udugov told Reuters.
A recent opinion poll showed Lebed was the most trusted politician in Russia.
Tens of thousands of people, mainly civilians, died in the 21-month Chechen conflict launched in December 1994 when Russia sent troops to quell the southern region's independence bid.
